https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Pacific Islands leaders and delegates arrive at Palau International Airport ahead of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting. Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Pacific Islands leaders and delegates arrive at Palau International Airport ahead of the 55th Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting. Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images Pacific Islands Forum Pacific Islands Forum meeting in turmoil after several leaders pull out of Palau summit Solomon Islands prime minister cancels his appearance, along with leaders from Fiji, Vanuatu and Samoa Krishani Dhanji and Australian Associated Press Sun 30 Aug 2026 03.22 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 06.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Several leaders have pulled out of a the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau at the eleventh hour. Solomon Islands prime minister, Matthew Wale, has cancelled his appearance after a no-confidence motion was lodged against him at home by the Solomon Islands home affairs minister, Manasseh Maelanga. Maelanga accused Wale of “repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance”, according to the ABC . Australia has been in negotiations with the Solomons on a security treaty, with the hope that further negotiations could have taken place on the sidelines of the summit. Fiji’s prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, will also not be attending, with the Samoan leader, La’auli Leuatea Schmidt, another notable absence. The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has confirmed he will still be attending. Oliver Nobetau, the Lowy Institute’s Pacific Islands program director, said the pulling out by key leaders “dulls the flame” of the meeting. “This has been shaping up to be quite a significant PIF … it’s really unfortunate that this is the case,” he told Guardian Australia. “With the pulling out of this many key prime ministers within the region, it dilutes the potential of what could come out of this leaders’ meeting.” Nobetau said there were high expectations that this leaders’ meeting could progress pilot projects around Pacific climate resilience, and was important ahead of the Cop31 climate summit in November and a pre-Cop31 summit to be held in Fiji and Tuvalu in October. He added the leaders not showing up could be read as those nations prioritising bilateral agreements with nations including Australia above region-wide commitments. “PIF has to demonstrate its usefulness as well. While it is a useful forum for a lot of our Pacific members, maybe the bigger countries feel there are more pressing issues or they can achieve more benefits for their countries by engaging bilaterally or directly with other partners.” Speaking at Queensland Labor conference on Sunday in Brisbane, Albanese said Australia had a duty to help Pacific nations thrive. Albanese said allowing Pacific nations to succeed would also benefit Australia. “The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific,” he told the “Australia has a key role to play, as a partner and leader. “In a time of strategic competition in our region, our engagement in the Pacific Islands Forum and our contributions to the infrastructure, regional security and climate action of the region matter more than ever before.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekdays Sign up to Afternoon Update Our Australian afternoon update breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The visit follows the prime minister signing a security deal with Fiji, elevating the bilateral relationship to a formal alliance as Australia seeks to curb Chinese influence in the region. Pacific leaders are set to discuss security and climate concerns during the summit. Albanese said Australia would also seek to reiterate support for Pacific workers coming to the country. Debate has recently raged over how the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility Scheme cohort would factor into immigration cuts flagged by various parties. Representatives of the resurgent One Nation have been pressed to clarify that PALM workers, many of whom provide much-needed labour in regional areas, would not be included in a significant reduction to net overseas migration. Albanese said the migration discussion had been fuelling division and the Pacific worker scheme would continue because of its critical economic benefit. “People from the Pacific make an enormous contribution to Australia’s prosperity through their vital work in regional industries like agriculture and meat processing,” he said. “So many of our farmers and food producers rely on them. “We know also the wages they remit home help boost the economies of their families and communities, contributing to the prosperity and stability of the whole region.” Explore more on these topics Pacific Islands Forum Pacific islands South Pacific Fiji Samoa Vanuatu news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world.text: Thank you for registering Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in Swipe for next article T he Kremlin ’s reaction to news that British-built long-range drones had been used in the latest Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory was predictably furious . And once again it came with a threat of retaliation . “The United Kingdom is acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks committed by Ukrainian neo-Nazis,” thundered the Russian Embassy in London in a statement. “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer … The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support of Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.” open image in gallery Putin has threatened the UK with ‘serious consequences’ after British-built drones were used to attack deep inside Russian territory ( Reuters ) This is by no means the first time blustering threats of this sort have been directed at the UK. Soon after Boris Johnson emerged as one of the most energetic cheerleaders for Ukraine in the wake of Putin’s February 2022 invasion, Kremlin media began to issue regular, blood-curdling warnings to London. Firebrand pro-war TV presenter Vladimir Solovyov spoke often and fondly of nuking the UK with Sarmat missiles – which he was convinced would sink the British Isles beneath the waves. “Give the British three days to learn to breathe underwater,” Solovyov ranted. His Rossiya 1 colleague Olga Skabeeva regularly hosted guests who – flatteringly for our security services – often spoke of Whitehall and MI6 as the true evil masterminds behind all Western policy. Such accusations were followed, more often than not, by the usual threats to nuke Perfidious Albion into non-existence. Recommended Putin’s empty threats to the UK are the last gasp of a dying Russia Putin is an open threat to the UK – will his admirer Nigel Farage finally say so? Russia is increasing its attacks on Ukrainian civilians – the West must respond It’s easy to see why the UK is the focus for the Kremlin’s attack dogs. Firstly, Russians have a long and deep love-hate relationship with Britain ’s legendary spies and fictional detectives. Secondly, compared to the US, the UK is unimportant and can be kicked about with impunity – whereas the Kremlin has an important and complicated on-again, off-again relationship with Donald Trump’s White House. But the problem for Britain’s security chiefs is that not all Russia’s threats are empty. Ken McCallum, director-general of MI5 warned in his annual threat update last October that “my teams are routinely uncovering attempts by state actors to commission surveillance, sabotage, arson or physical violence, right here in the UK”. He also warned that Russian spy agencies were hiring thugs online to do their dirty work, “instructing them via encrypted apps, and offering payment in cryptocurrencies”. These were the kinds of desperadoes who were responsible for the first major Kremlin-orchestrated physical attack on UK soil since the Ukraine invasion, when a warehouse in Leyton, London, tied to a Ukrainian-owned business went up in flames in March 2024 . Of the seven people charged with aggravated arson and accepting payment from a foreign intelligence agency, several admitted carrying out the attack on behalf of Russia. Another fire was started at a DHL transport warehouse in Minworth, Birmingham, in July 2024 when a package detonated after arriving from Vilnius. Lithuanian prosecutors uncovered a Europe-wide plot by Russia’s GU military intelligence to sabotage DHL centres with similar parcel bombs in Leipzig and Warsaw. open image in gallery 2024: Firefighters tackle a blaze following a Kremlin-orchestrated attack on a warehouse in Leyton, London ( London Fire Brigade ) Other plots thwarted by MI5 include the “Minions” case when a senior Russian espionage officer recruited a gang of dim-bulb Eastern European crooks in London with the intention of assassinating journalists and activists hostile to the Kremlin. Another involved a gang tasked with organising arson attacks on Sir Keir Starmer’s car and former residence. Two men were convicted after being recruited by a Russian-speaking online handler who was linked to a pro-Kremlin sabotage network, although the criminal proceedings did not establish that the Russian state itself ordered the attacks So far, so pathetic. It’s not clear what the Kremlin’s aggravated hooliganism is intended to achieve – except to confirm how powerless, stupid and desperate the successors of the once-mighty KGB have become. And yet there are very real, and very much more dangerous, weapons in Russia’s covert arsenal that lie just a couple of levels of escalation away. open image in gallery ‘We see you’: a Russian spy-ship was spotted lurking in British waters earlier this year ( UK MoD/Crown copyright ) In April, the Yantar – a Russian spy-ship posing as an oceanographical vessel – was spotted lurking along the British coast. Such vessels were “designed to survey underwater infrastructure during peacetime, and sabotage it in conflict”, said then-defence secretary John Healey, directly warning the Kremlin that “ we see you, we see your activity over our cables and pipelines. And you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated.” Britain and Ireland’s electricity, internet and gas supplies all depend on a network of fragile and unprotected undersea cables that can easily be blown up or simply cut by dragging anchors – as sporadic supposedly “accidental” damage to cables between Finland and Estonia in recent years has shown. There’s also been a disturbing escalation last week when a small drone carrying explosives was intercepted at Leipzig airport in Germany – a major logistics hub for the international shipping company DHL as well as Ukrainian-operated aircraft. While there’s no smoking gun linking this attempted attack to Russia (yet), blowing up a civilian aircraft at a European airport would come very close to an act of war. There are very real, and very much more dangerous, weapons in Russia’s covert arsenal that lie just a couple of levels of escalation away But it’s Britain, not Germany, that many Russian “Z-bloggers” consider a combatant in the Ukraine war. That’s because the UK is the only one of Kyiv’s international allies which has allowed its weaponry - first Storm Shadow cruise missiles and, now, BAe-made Nyan drones – to be used in Ukrainian attacks inside Russia itself. Germany and the US, by contrast, have refused to allow their ATACMs rocket artillery or Taurus cruise missiles to be used in deep strikes precisely for fear of triggering escalation, restricting their weaponry solely to battlefields in Russian-occupied Ukraine. Does that make Britain a combatant against Russia – and, by extension, a legitimate military target? The Kremlin faces a dilemma when it comes to responding to the Nyan strikes . Militarily, the small British drone makes little difference to Ukraine’s world-leading military drone production, which is expected to reach 7 million units by the end of this year. Yet at the same time the UK is the biggest cash contributor to Ukraine’s war effort now that Trump has cut off US funding almost entirely. Would some kind of attack on Britain scare Andrew Burnham’s new government into pulling back its support for Kyiv – or would it, conversely, unite Europe and Nato into intensifying and escalating its support for Ukraine? Burnham responded defiantly to the Kremlin’s threats, insisting that the “UK is doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin .” He described the use of British-made Nyan jet-propelled drones as “support so that Ukraine can defend itself” and vowed that Britain was not a “fair-weather friend … and that won’t change”. open image in gallery Burnham reiterated Britain’s support for Ukraine after the Kremlin’s threats ( PA ) That’s easy to say as long as Russian interventions remain on the level of minor arson attacks ineptly executed by mercenary morons. But what if the kind of assassination plot that German police uncovered against Armin Papperger, CEO of Germany’s Rheinmetall arms corporation, in 2024, becomes a deadly reality on British soil? Or if a DHL cargo plane explodes on the runway at Birmingham Airport, or the vital connectors linking the UK and France’s electrical grids are “accidentally” severed by a tanker’s seven-ton anchor? If the Kremlin’s threatened “price” is a direct challenge to escalate all the way to the brink of a shooting war, will Burnham be able to persuade the British people that their country should go to war over a disputed sliver of Ukraine? Recommended Putin is a ‘cornered rat’ – here’s why that’s bad news for Ukraine – and us Andy Burnham has just found out that pranksters are no laughing matter Donald Trump has found exciting new ways to embarrass America – can this one man stop him? So far, such an escalation remains remote – but only because Putin believes that his army’s slow advance across Donbas means that he will eventually crush Ukraine’s resistance. However, as I wrote last month for The Independent , trouble for Putin is much closer to home, with increasing tensions inside Russia’s elite between business interests exhausted by the war and those securocrats who owe power and incomes to continued conflict. A cornered, desperate Putin will be far more dangerous, and more unpredictable and last month two senior Kremlin sources, one of whom meets regularly with the president, were quoted as saying they predicted a “high probability” of escalation in the coming months. Two things are clear – one, that Britain is extremely vulnerable and unprepared for attack , whether it’s in cyberspace or on its critical infrastructure. The other is that Russian spies and soldiers have been methodically probing our weaknesses, ready to strike if and when the Kremlin grows sufficiently reckless to give the order. Bolojan says that although Romania managed to absorb only 90% of the funds allotted through this programme, over 2 thousand projects were not finalized by August 31, the EU deadline of finalizing and meeting all the milestones, targets and PNRR-funded projects. Romania’s Parliament has urgently endorsed a law under which the works done after August 31, are no longer covered from EU funds, but will be covered from local and state budgets or from other funds. If the beneficiaries do not finish them by December 31, 2026, they will have to return all the money they received. SESSION Romania’s two-chamber Parliament kicked off its autumn session on Tuesday. The first day was dedicated to electing the leadership of both chambers and of the party representatives to the permanent bureaus. Key priorities for the session include the vote on a new government with full powers, the reorganisation of the public administration of state-owned enterprises and electoral reform. Other topics on its agenda are the unified wage system in the public sector and healthcare system funding, as well as the high school admission system in the field of education. Romania has had a caretaker government since May 5, when the minority cabinet formed by the National Liberal Party, the Save Romania Union and the Democratic Union of Ethnic Hungarians in Romania and led by the Liberal leader Ilie Bolojan was dismissed by Parliament in a vote of no-confidence. After MEP Eugen Tomac, initially designated as the prime ministerial candidate withdrew, dissident Liberal Adrian Veştea was nominated but failed to secure the necessary endorsements in Parliament. TALKS Romanian Interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan held a telephone conversation on Tuesday with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte regarding key security challenges in the region, focusing on the war in Ukraine and the security situation in the Black Sea. The Romanian official emphasized the need for the Alliance to maintain its focus on the Eastern Flank and the Black Sea—including through the deployment of Allied capabilities to Romania—amidst intensifying drone incursions into national maritime and airspace. Also on Tuesday, Ilie Bolojan spoke by phone with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, discussing regional security developments and key areas of cooperation between Romania and Ukraine. Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan reaffirmed Romania’s solidarity with and support for Ukraine and expressed appreciation for the sacrifices made by the Ukrainian people in the face of Russian aggression. CHANCELLOR The Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel was received on Tuesday by the President of Romania, Nicușor Dan. Their discussions focused on the international political and security context, European Union solidarity, and the need for European states to assume greater responsibility within NATO. The former German Chancellor is in Bucharest to present her memoir, *Freedom: Memories 1954–2021*. The book was launched internationally in 2024 across more than 30 countries. Bucharest is one of the few locations—alongside capitals such as Berlin, Washington, Budapest, and Athens—where the former Chancellor chose to attend the book presentation in person. In the book, she reflects on her childhood and youth spent in the so-called German Democratic Republic—a communist satellite of the Soviet Union—the fall of the Berlin Wall, and the beginnings of her political career; she also offers insight into the decisions made during her 16 years leading the German government and her meetings with leaders on the international stage. Angela Merkel served as Chancellor of Germany from 2005 to 2021, becoming the first woman to hold the office. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/germany-s.text: Charlie Bradley, Ciaran McGrath Updated Mon, September 14, 2026 at 1:10 PM UTC 1 German troops (Image: Getty) Germany is poised to send 1,000 soldiers to NATO 's eastern flank amid fears Russia could launch an attack or even an invasion into the Baltic states. Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has ordered that the first compulsory assignments begin by the end of September, according to an exclusive report by the German newspaper BILD. The move comes as Berlin races to establish a permanent military presence on NATO's eastern flank. Germany plans to have 4,800 troops permanently stationed in Lithuania by the end of 2027 as part of its commitment to strengthen the alliance's defences in the Baltic region. However, recruitment for the brigade has fallen far short of requirements, with only about 60% of the necessary posts filled by volunteers. Germany's Defence Minister Boris Pistorius (Image: Getty) The biggest shortages are understood to be among IT specialists, logistics personnel, cooks and other ranks. BILD reports that around 20% of the brigade's posts could currently be affected by compulsory assignments, although the Bundeswehr hopes to reduce that figure to 10% by the end of September. Pistorius had previously acknowledged that compulsory assignments could be necessary, telling BILD that he expected the number affected to be below 1,000. The principle of voluntary service remains in place, but the German defence ministry says compulsory assignments are necessary to ensure the brigade is operational. The Bundeswehr has spent months trying to persuade troops to volunteer for the move, including through advertising campaigns and familiarisation trips to Lithuania for soldiers and their families. However, time is now running short, with the brigade not due to be fully established until the end of 2027. Soldiers selected for compulsory deployment will be informed and have the opportunity to take legal action against the decision. They will also need time to organise a potential move to Lithuania, adding to the pressure on Berlin as it attempts to fill the remaining gaps in the force. The development comes amid heightened tensions on NATO's eastern flank, with Lithuania among the alliance's Baltic members closest to Russia.
